extracted.intended_audience: maritime lawyers, judges, law students, and merchants concerned with wartime commerce and prize law
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory legal treatise setting out rules and principles governing the effects of war on commerce and shipping, as applied by maritime tribunals and courts. Includes definitions (e.g., solemn war), procedural effects (declarations, manifestoes), property and contract consequences, and doctrines on insurance, bills, and prize practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: International legislator / interpreter
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no general body that can legislate on the Law of Nations; maritime tribunals of maritime states are almost the sole interpreters and mouthpieces of international law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parliaments, sovereigns, and congresses cannot create universal law binding other nations; national statutes affecting foreigners are valid only if consistent with the Law of Nations. Quotes Lord Stowell to emphasize judicial impartiality and universality of international law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source and foundation of the Law of Nations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Law of Nations is founded on general principles of right and justice and the public opinion of the civilized world as it stands when a case arises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To ascertain it, consult theoretical writings, history, judicial decisions, treaties, and modern usage. A doctrine fairly deduced from rights, duties, and moral obligations of nations may belong to the Law of Nations even if not universally recognized.

rubrics_metrics.name: How international law may be updated
rubrics_metrics.description: International tribunals may alter or enunciate new rules when modern public and international opinion justify change; they may also refuse to alter settled rules if they remain deducible from foundational principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of modern opinion includes abandonment of a practice, numerous treaties, or extension of modern moral principles. Examples cited: condemnation of letters of marque/privateers, slave trade rulings, salvage for recapture, and denials of certain confiscation rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Public / Solemn War
rubrics_metrics.description: Solemn (Public and Solemn) War requires (1) contending parties to be nations or allied nations acting under a supreme executive, and (2) proclamation, notification, or declaration; usually general rather than merely local or defensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish from imperfect wars (reprisals/acts of hostility) which are public but not solemn and may be treated differently for legal purposes such as dating commencement of war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declarations of war are not strictly necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: A Declaration of War is not necessary to legalize hostilities; acts of hostilities without declaration are lawful unless committed in manifest bad faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nevertheless, a declaration can itself create a state of war and fix the date from which legal consequences flow; declarations are useful to distinguish lawful acts of war from naked wrongs when peace is reestablished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manifesto (contents and function)
rubrics_metrics.description: A manifesto/ declaration announces the commencement and existence of hostilities, states reasons and attempts justification, instructs subjects on intercourse with the foe, and notifies neutrals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to fix the date of commencement of hostilities; when issued it 'legalizes' acts and breaches done under pressure of war. Important for merchants and neutrals to conform conduct to new rights/duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of declaration: war between every subject of the states
rubrics_metrics.description: When war is duly declared, the war is between nation and nation; every individual of one state is enemy to every individual of the other, with many consequential rights and duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle underlies rules on seizure, trading, and legal incapacities (e.g., alien enemies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seizure rule for enemy persons and property found in belligerent territory at outbreak
rubrics_metrics.description: On principle enemy persons and property in belligerent territory are liable to detention and confiscation, but modern international usage generally exempts persons and property found within the territory at the commencement of hostilities from seizure as prize of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This usage is often enforced by treaty but is not an immutable rule; sovereigns may follow or abandon it at will; applicability may vary by jurisdiction and circumstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for immoveable property
rubrics_metrics.description: Immoveable things (e.g., landed estates) possessed in a belligerent's country are not confiscated by declaration of war, although income from them may be sequestrated to prevent remittance to the enemy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiates treatment of land from movable property and highlights measures short of confiscation to block benefits going to enemy owners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of public funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Public funds (debts due from a sovereign to private persons) are ordinarily protected from confiscation in war, upheld as a matter of public faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only rare historical exceptions exist; courts should avoid inquiry into whether part of public debt is due to enemy subjects during war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of reciprocity
rubrics_metrics.description: Treatment of enemy property at the commencement of war often follows reciprocity—this country will condemn property seized before the war if the enemy condemns, and restore if the enemy restores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctioned by authority (Sir William Scott) and connected to broad principles (e.g., Magna Charta). Courts and governments may apply reciprocity in prize decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Droits of Admiralty and prize jurisdiction in ports
rubrics_metrics.description: Prize Courts have tried captures made in ports, havens, or rivers within the realm; ships of the enemy may be detained in ports and condemned as enemy property despite being in port at outbreak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical effect: captures in territorially enclosed waters are subject to Admiralty jurisdiction; detention of ships without knowledge of hostilities may nevertheless result in condemnation absent reciprocal arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hostile embargo as reprisal
rubrics_metrics.description: Seizing and detaining enemy ships in ports (hostile embargo) is a species of reprisal and may be used even when such seizures conflict with liberal principles protecting property brought in confidence of peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practice is reproached as against modern liberality but has been used by many European states; England historically may have been less influenced by enemy reciprocity in this respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debts due to and from enemy during war
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequestration of debts due from one sovereign to subjects of the enemy as retaliation has occurred (e.g., Danish ordinance), but English courts have held such ordinances not a legal defence to suit in England and not conformable to the Law of Nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The right to confiscate debts is contested historically and not generally recognized in modern practice; rule may vary by country (possible US differences noted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interruption of intercourse; trading with the enemy unlawful absent licence
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial intercourse between subjects of belligerent states is generally completely interrupted and unlawful after war begins, except under special licence from the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereign alone may permit partial commercial intercourse (homeward trade etc.); private persons cannot decide to trade with enemy without exposing property to confiscation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royal licence and homeward trade exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Trading with the enemy is unlawful except under Royal Licence; where government authorises homeward trade it may not have authorised outward trade and outward voyages may remain illegal and cargo liable to confiscation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases show cargoes purchased before war but shipped after declaration have been condemned; merchants should seek special governmental permission to withdraw goods from enemy territory safely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects of an ally during conjoint war
rubrics_metrics.description: In a conjoint (allied) war, subjects of an ally cannot trade with the common enemy without liability to forfeiture of property in the prize courts of the ally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permission to relax this rule can come only from the allied sovereigns by mutual consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracts made during war are void
rubrics_metrics.description: All contracts made with the enemy during war are void—this includes insurances on the enemy's property, drawing/negotiation of bills of exchange involving the enemy, sending money or bills to the enemy country, and commercial partnerships; attempts to evade by third parties are equally illegal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voidness is by public policy of war; courts nevertheless sometimes recognize residual obligations or promises after peace; contracts in contemplation of war designed to evade belligerent rights are also illegal even if made by neutrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insurance voidness for voyages prohibited by law
rubrics_metrics.description: An insurance contract is vacated and annulled ab initio wherever an insurance is made on a voyage expressly prohibited by common, statute, or maritime law of the country (e.g., voyages to an enemy's garrison or contrary to express act/proclamation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validity of a policy is tested by the voyage (public policy), not merely by parties' intentions. Policies to ambiguous destinations (e.g., 'ports in the Baltic') may be valid if not necessarily hostile. Insurance on neutral vessels carrying contraband may be affected by cargo legality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insurances and contraband / neutral colonial trade nuance
rubrics_metrics.description: Insurances on neutral vessels carrying contraband goods are affected by the illegality of the cargo; insurances on neutral vessels engaged in the colonial trade of an enemy (closed to neutrals in peace) may be valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether insurance is void depends on whether the illegality concerns the voyage or the cargo; goods purchased using proceeds of a former illegal voyage may nevertheless be insurable in the reverse direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bills of exchange drawn during war (general rule and exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bills drawn or negotiated with the enemy are null and void if instrumental in assisting communication with the enemy; however, courts have allowed limited exceptions (e.g., bills for subsistence of detained nationals) and held that void bills may form the basis of a post-peace promise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key test: whether the bill facilitates communication or commerce with the enemy. Liberal application may permit necessary subsistence arrangements for prisoners; complex examples indicate nuance in enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of declaration on contracts made before war
rubrics_metrics.description: If performance of a contract entered into before the war is rendered unlawful by government measures (e.g., interdiction of a voyage), the contract is dissolved on both sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by affreightment contracts: if voyage becomes unlawful or interdicted or is completely defeated by capture, the contract is dissolved. Courts consider whether a complete defeat of the undertaking has occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voyage defeated by capture dissolves contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a voyage is broken up by capture on the passage, so as to cause a complete defeat of the undertaking, the contract (e.g., affreightment) is dissolved notwithstanding other considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus is on practical impossibility of performance rather than mere delay; capture that makes completion impossible discharges contractual obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining modern public opinion for legal change
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern international opinion is ascertained by: universal abandonment of a practice, numerous treaties, and application of improved moral principles to international relations; judges must look to contemporary feeling when deciding whether to adapt or overrule past rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges should bring all necessary knowledge into court and, if they see departure from past sense of right, make modern sense the fountain of modern law; precedents remain persuasive but not absolute.
